where: Section 1, the sentence starting 'A short wavelength has a wider mode field'
problem: The physics is backwards. The mode field widens as wavelength increases; at short wavelengths the mode is tighter and better confined (bend loss of the fundamental grows with wavelength). The looped trace drops at short wavelengths because below cutoff a weakly confined higher-order mode (LP11) is still guided and the bend strips it, not because short wavelengths are weakly confined.
fix: Below cutoff the fiber still guides a weakly confined higher-order mode, and the bend strips that mode, so the looped trace loses power. Above cutoff only the fundamental mode is left, it is well confined, and the bend removes very little, so the gap closes. Bend sensitivity of the fundamental itself grows with wavelength because the mode field widens.

where: Section 1, 'Launch the same broad-spectrum source into two samples'
problem: Two separate samples of fiber are not comparable; the straight and looped traces must come from the same fiber, otherwise the difference reflects fiber-to-fiber variation.
fix: Launch the broad-spectrum source into one length of fiber and record the trace straight and then with one loop, comparing the two traces of the same fiber.

problem: The text tells the student to report the loop diameter but never gives the standard value, so the student cannot tell whether a reported diameter is normal.
fix: Add that the standard transmission method uses a loop of 60 mm radius, and that the 2 m measurement gives the fiber cutoff wavelength while a longer cabled length gives the cable cutoff, which is shorter.

problem: 'Above cutoff the core guides the fundamental mode' suggests the fundamental is not guided below cutoff, which is wrong; it is guided on both sides of cutoff.
fix: Below cutoff a weakly confined higher-order mode also propagates and the bend strips it; above cutoff that mode is no longer guided, only the well-confined fundamental remains, and the two traces meet.

where: Section 1, 'The index profile gives the same value'
problem: The far-field 5% value and the profile value agree only approximately; the far-field NA usually comes out a little larger because of launch and mode-excitation effects. 'The same value' reads as exact equality.
fix: Say the index profile gives approximately the same value, NA = √(n1² − n2²), with n1 the core index and n2 the cladding index, and expect a small difference from the far-field number.
